name: Umami, the savory fifth taste
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: The 'deliciousness' taste and where it hides. T1: there are five basic tastes, and the deep savory one you meet in broth, parmesan, and a ripe tomato is UMAMI (Japanese for 'deliciousness'). T1: umami is what makes food seem 'meaty' or 'rich' even in a bowl of clear, meatless broth. T2: chemist Kikunae Ikeda tracked it down in 1908 by boiling down KOMBU (kelp) dashi and isolating the molecule GLUTAMATE. T2: the tongue has a dedicated umami receptor (T1R1+T1R3) — it is a genuine basic taste, not a blend of the other four. T3: MSG is just that umami molecule sold as a seasoning — Ikeda's firm Ajinomoto marketed monosodium glutamate; the old 'MSG scare' was never substantiated. T3: foods get intensely savory as they AGE or ripen because proteins break down into FREE glutamate — a green tomato has little, a sun-ripened one plenty. T4: umami hides in surprising non-meat foods loaded with free glutamate — aged parmesan, dried shiitake, anchovies, soy sauce, Marmite, even breast milk. T4: umami is why a splash of fish sauce or a parmesan rind makes a vegetable dish taste 'meaty' with no meat in it. T5: SYNERGY — Japanese dashi stacks kombu's glutamate with bonito-flake inosinate, and the two together taste many times more savory than either alone. T5: that same glutamate-plus-nucleotide synergy is why tomato-and-parmesan or mushroom-and-meat combos taste so deeply satisfying.
source: Wikipedia 'Umami' (consulted, confirms Ikeda 1908 / kombu / glutamate / TAS1R1+TAS1R3 / free-glutamate foods incl. parmesan, shiitake, tomato, breast milk); glutamate+inosinate umami synergy (dashi) well documented.
framing_note: Wonder voice: lead with the mystery 'why does a clear, meatless broth taste so rich?' — never 'What is umami?'. Accuracy rail: umami was isolated by Ikeda in 1908 from KOMBU (kelp), NOT bonito — bonito is the SECOND, synergistic source; keep MSG framed factually (safe seasoning; the 'MSG scare' was never borne out). Dinner-test payoff = the T5 dashi-synergy rung (two savory foods multiply each other).

name: The five basic tastes and the tongue-map myth
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: What the tongue can and can't actually do. T1: there are FIVE basic tastes the tongue detects — sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami — and nearly everything else we call 'flavor' comes from smell. T1: the famous 'tongue map' (sweet on the tip, bitter at the back) is a MYTH — every basic taste is detected all over the tongue. T2: SOUR is the tongue sensing ACID (hydrogen ions) — which is why lemons, vinegar, and sour candy all share that same pucker. T2: SALTY is literally the tongue detecting sodium ions through a specific channel, which is why other 'salts' taste off rather than salty. T3: BITTER is caught by about 25 different receptors — far more than any other taste — because there are so many different natural poisons to catch. T3: taste buds aren't only on the tongue; they also line the roof of the mouth and throat, and each bud packs 50-100 taste cells. T4: your taste cells are replaced every week or two — you constantly regrow your entire sense of taste. T4: 'spicy' and 'minty-cool' are NOT tastes at all — chili and mint fool the touch/temperature nerves, not the taste buds. T4: fizzy CARBONATION is read by the SOUR cells — an enzyme on them turns the drink's CO2 into acid, so soda's 'bite' is partly a sour taste, not just bubbles.
source: Wikipedia 'Taste' (five basic tastes; tongue-map is a debunked myth; bud anatomy/turnover); Chandrashekar et al., Science 2009 'The Taste of Carbonation' (CO2 sensed via carbonic anhydrase on sour cells).
framing_note: Scene-led: open on 'draw the tongue map you learned in school — and you'll get it wrong' to invert the famous myth. Accuracy rail: the tongue-map is FALSE (all tastes are detected everywhere); the five are sweet/sour/salty/bitter/umami, and 'spicy'/'cool' are touch-temperature sensations, NOT tastes. Dinner-test payoff = the tongue-map-is-a-myth rung (T1), with the carbonation-tasted-as-sour rung (T4) as the sleeper.

name: Capsaicin and TRPV1, the burn that isn't heat
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Why chili 'burns' when nothing is actually hot. T1: chili peppers feel HOT even at room temperature, but there's no real heat — the burn is a trick played on your nerves. T1: the molecule behind it is CAPSAICIN, concentrated in the pale ribs and pith inside the pepper (not mainly the seeds). T2: capsaicin latches onto TRPV1, the very same nerve sensor that fires when your mouth touches something painfully hot (around 43C / 110F). T2: so your brain gets the identical 'I'm burning!' alarm it would from scalding food — with zero actual damage. T3: WATER barely helps; MILK works because its protein CASEIN grabs the oily capsaicin and lifts it off your receptors — capsaicin is oil-soluble, and oil and water don't mix. T3: David Julius won the 2021 Nobel Prize for discovering that TRPV1 is the heat sensor capsaicin hijacks. T4: BIRDS feel no burn at all — their version of TRPV1 ignores capsaicin — which is exactly the plant's plan: birds swallow and scatter seeds intact while chewing mammals are warned off. T4: the SCOVILLE scale rates a pepper's heat by how much sugar-water it takes to dilute it until you can no longer taste the burn (Wilbur Scoville, 1912). T5: the pain triggers an ENDORPHIN rush — the body's own painkillers — which is why chili-lovers get a genuine pleasant high from a fiery meal ('benign masochism'). T5: because TRPV1 is a heat sensor, chili feels hotter in warm food, and its burn fades over a meal as the receptors get worn out.
source: Wikipedia 'TRPV1' (consulted: capsaicin binds TRPV1; ~43C threshold; David Julius 2021 Nobel); milk/casein studies (milkgenomics.org; PMC 'Putting out the fire — efficacy of common beverages in reducing oral burn from capsaicin'); Jordt & Julius, Cell 2002 'Molecular Basis for Species-Specific Sensitivity to Hot Chili Peppers' (birds/seed dispersal).
framing_note: Prep/eating-voice is fine ('you bite into the chili'). Wonder inversion: hook with 'your mouth screams burning but a thermometer reads normal.' Accuracy rails: capsaicin lives mostly in the RIBS/pith, not chiefly the seeds; MILK (casein), NOT water, cuts it; TRPV1's ~43C threshold; birds are immune BY DESIGN (seed dispersal). Dinner-test payoff = the birds-are-immune / seed-dispersal rung (T4).

name: Smell is flavor (retronasal olfaction)
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: The secret that most of 'taste' isn't taste at all. T1: pinch your nose, eat a jelly bean, and you get only 'sweet' — let go and the CHERRY floods in; most of what we call flavor is actually SMELL. T1: that's exactly why food tastes flat and boring when you have a stuffy cold. T2: the tongue only reports the five basic tastes; everything specific — strawberry, coffee, bacon — is your nose reading aromas. T2: scientists estimate flavor is roughly 80% smell (Yale's Gordon Shepherd). T3: chewing pushes aromas UP the back of the throat into the nose from the inside — this is 'retronasal' smell, a different route than sniffing a flower from outside ('orthonasal'). T3: because of that route, the very same molecule can smell one way when you sniff it and 'taste' different while you're eating it. T4: 'flavor' is really taste + smell + touch + temperature all bundled by the brain into a single experience. T4: warm food is more flavorful than cold because heat releases more aroma molecules to float up to your nose. T5: the brain even has a flavor region that fires only for retronasal smell, treating mouth-aromas as their own sense. T5: it's also why holding your nose lets you gulp down a food or medicine you find disgusting — you've muted the 80% that is smell.
source: Boston Globe 'Mapping the flow of flavor particles' and Yale Scientific Magazine (jelly-bean/nose-pinch demo; Gordon Shepherd ~80% figure; nasopharynx route); PMC 'Retronasal odor perception requires taste cortex but orthonasal does not' (retronasal vs orthonasal distinct).
framing_note: Scene-led with the nose-pinch jelly-bean demo a kid can run tonight. Accuracy rail: the tongue detects only the five basic tastes; specific 'flavors' are RETRONASAL smell (~80%), a distinct path from sniffing (orthonasal) — don't call flavor a tongue phenomenon. Dinner-test payoff = the pinch-your-nose jelly-bean rung (T1), instantly testable at the table.

name: Supertasters and the bitter gene
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Why your kid gags at broccoli and you don't. T1: people live in different taste worlds — to some, plain broccoli or black coffee tastes screamingly BITTER; to others it's mild. T1: the strong reactors are called SUPERTASTERS, and it's largely something you're born with, not fussiness. T2: it comes down to a bitter-detecting gene (TAS2R38) that reads compounds in broccoli, kale, and grapefruit — supertasters carry the sensitive version. T2: scientists spot supertasters with a harmless bitter test strip (PROP/PTC) — 'nontasters' taste plain paper, supertasters taste something vile. T3: supertasters also have MORE taste buds packed on the tongue (the little bumps called fungiform papillae) — dye the tongue blue and you can literally count them. T3: it's not all upside — supertasters often shun bitter vegetables AND find chili, fat, and sweets more intense than everyone else. T4: KIDS are extra bitter-sensitive by nature and mostly grow out of it — an evolutionary guard so toddlers spit out toxic plants.
source: Linda Bartoshuk (Yale) coined 'supertaster' 1991; PMC 'Bitter Receptor Gene (TAS2R38), PROP Bitterness' (TAS2R38 PAV/AVI haplotypes, PROP/PTC probes, fungiform-papillae density); PubMed 29729324 'The development of basic taste sensitivity and preferences in children.'
framing_note: Wonder voice: open on 'why does the same broccoli taste fine to Dad and vile to his kid?'. Accuracy rail: supertasting is largely genetic (TAS2R38 plus papillae density), NOT preference or being picky; frame kid bitter-sensitivity as normal developmental biology, no moralizing about fussy eaters. Dinner-test payoff = the blue-dye-and-count-your-taste-buds rung (T3).

name: Acquired tastes, bitterness as a poison alarm
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Why nobody's first sip of coffee is 'yum.' T1: almost no one enjoys black coffee, dark beer, or unsweetened dark chocolate the first time — they taste harshly bitter. T1: that's by design: BITTER is the body's built-in poison alarm, because most natural poisons taste bitter. T2: yet the mouth never stops reporting 'bitter' — coffee tastes just as bitter to a lifelong drinker as to a first-timer. T2: what changes is the BRAIN — it learns the bitter drink is safe and comes with a reward (caffeine's lift, beer's buzz), so it re-labels the taste as pleasant. T3: this learned liking needs REPEATED exposure — 'acquired taste' is literally your brain updating after many tries, not your tongue toughening up. T3: the reward is the teacher — we acquire tastes for coffee, beer, and chili partly because each delivers a payoff the brain starts to crave. T4: tonic water's quinine and grapefruit's bite are the same story — genuinely toxin-associated flavors we learn to enjoy in safe amounts. T4: it's why grown-up bitter treats are paired with sugar or fat (dark chocolate, coffee with cream) — the reward coaxes the brain into accepting the alarm.
source: ScienceDaily/EurekAlert 'Avoiding poisons: a matter of bitter taste' and Duke Health 'Toxins drove evolution of human taste' (bitter = poison-avoidance); ScienceABC & Colby 'mere-exposure effect' pieces + PMC 'How we learn to like' (conditioned taste preference: tongue signal unchanged, brain hedonic value updates).
framing_note: Wonder voice: open on 'why is a child's face at their first taste of coffee always the same?'. Accuracy rail: the TONGUE keeps signaling bitter unchanged — it's the BRAIN's hedonic value that shifts with exposure and reward; do NOT say taste buds 'toughen up' or 'die off.' Dinner-test payoff = the 'coffee still tastes just as bitter — your brain simply changed its mind' rung (T2).

name: Why onions make you cry
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: The onion's chemical booby-trap. T1: a whole, uncut onion is nearly odorless and won't sting your eyes — the tears only start when you CUT it and break the cells open. T1: slicing lets two chemicals the onion kept apart inside its cells finally mix and react — like snapping a glow-stick. T2: the reaction releases a volatile SULFUR gas (a 'lachrymatory factor') that drifts up toward your eyes. T2: in the thin watery film on your eyeball, that gas turns into a weak SULFURIC ACID — the sting your eyes frantically flush out with tears. T3: it's a plant DEFENSE — the onion evolved this to punish animals that bite into its bulb. T3: tricks that actually work: CHILL the onion (cold slows the reaction and the gas), use a razor-SHARP knife (less crushing means less gas), and cut near a fan or flame. T4: scientists pinned down the exact enzyme that builds the tear-gas (lachrymatory-factor synthase), and 'tearless' onions have been bred by dialing it down. T4: garlic runs the very same chemistry for its punch — but garlic's reaction makes a compound that doesn't fly (allicin), so garlic bites your nose and tongue instead of your eyes.
source: University of Bristol 'Molecule of the Month: Propanethial S-oxide'; ACS Chemical Biology / PubMed 28708375 'Crystal Structure of Lachrymatory Factor Synthase from Allium cepa'; Library of Congress Everyday Mysteries 'Why does chopping an onion make you cry?'.
framing_note: Prep-voice is perfect ('as your knife slices through...'). Scene-led: hook on 'a whole onion never makes you cry — so what does the knife set loose?'. Accuracy rail: the irritant is a volatile SULFUR gas that becomes sulfuric acid IN the eye's moisture, and it forms only on cutting (cells must rupture) — not from the whole bulb. Dinner-test payoff = the chill-it / sharp-knife fixes rung (T3), usable tonight.

name: Cilantro tastes like soap
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Why some people swear cilantro is dish-soap. T1: to a large minority of people, fresh cilantro (coriander leaf) tastes like SOAP rather than herb — and they are not imagining it or being fussy. T1: those people literally SMELL something in cilantro that the rest of us don't. T2: cilantro leaves are packed with ALDEHYDE molecules — and that very same family of aldehydes is used to give many soaps their 'clean' smell. T2: the soap-tasters carry a version of a SMELL-receptor gene (OR6A2) that locks onto those aldehydes and shouts 'soap!'. T3: a huge DNA study (23andMe, tens of thousands of people) traced the soapy-cilantro reaction to a spot right next to a cluster of smell-receptor genes. T3: because it's mostly a SMELL trait, chopping or crushing cilantro — plus time and cooking — mellows it, since bruising breaks the aldehydes down.
source: Eriksson et al., Flavour 2012 'A genetic variant near olfactory receptor genes influences cilantro preference' (SNP rs72921001 near OR6A2; 23andMe GWAS, tens of thousands of participants); Cleveland Clinic / 23andMe blog (aldehydes shared with soap).
framing_note: Wonder voice: open on 'why do some people insist this fresh herb tastes like dish-soap?'. Accuracy rail: this is a SMELL-receptor (olfactory) genetics story — the aldehydes that cilantro and soap share — NOT a taste-bud difference or mere dislike; keep it non-judgmental toward the soap-tasters. Dinner-test payoff = the 'cilantro and soap literally share the same aldehyde molecules' rung (T2).

name: The Sichuan buzz, a molecule that vibrates your nerves
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: The peppercorn that makes your lips buzz. T1: Sichuan peppercorns don't burn like chili — they make your lips and tongue TINGLE, fizz, and go half-numb (the 'ma' in mala hot-pot). T1: it's a totally different sensation from chili heat, and Sichuan cooking stacks the two on purpose. T2: the molecule responsible is hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, and it doesn't fool a heat sensor or a taste bud at all — it hijacks your TOUCH nerves. T2: it makes the light-touch and vibration nerves in your lips fire as if something were physically buzzing against them. T3: scientists measured that phantom buzz and it feels like a vibration around 50 times a second — the very flutter those nerve endings are tuned to detect. T3: so the 'tingle' is your brain insisting your lips are being tapped rapidly when nothing is touching them at all. T4: chili (a heat sensor) and Sichuan pepper (touch nerves) light up completely separate systems — which is why mala food can feel fiery-hot AND buzzy at the same time.
source: Hagura et al., Proc. Royal Society B 2013 (sanshool tingle perceived at ~50 Hz, matching RA/Meissner light-touch channel); Bautista et al., Nature Neuroscience 2008 / PubMed 18568022 (sanshool excites sensory neurons via two-pore K+ channels); PMC 'Food vibrations: Asian spice sets lips trembling.'
framing_note: Wonder voice: hook on 'this peppercorn makes your lips buzz like a phone on vibrate.' Accuracy rail: sanshool works on TOUCH/vibration nerves (mechanoreceptors), NOT heat or taste — a distinct system from chili's heat sensor; keep '~50 times a second' as the vivid image, not a number the player must recall. Dinner-test payoff = the '~50-Hz phantom vibration your brain invents' rung (T3).

name: Taste-modifiers, molecules that hijack your sweet sensor
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Foods that rewire what your tongue reports. T1: the MIRACLE BERRY, a small red West-African fruit, briefly makes sour foods taste SWEET — a raw lemon becomes lemonade, vinegar tastes like apple juice. T1: the effect is temporary (about an hour) and the berry itself is barely sweet — it changes your tongue, it doesn't add sugar. T2: its protein, MIRACULIN, clamps onto your sweet receptors and switches them ON only when acid hits them — so sour reads as sweet until it wears off. T2: the opposite plant exists — an Indian leaf, Gymnema (gurmar, 'sugar destroyer'), blocks the sweet receptor so sugar tastes like flavorless sand for a while. T3: ARTICHOKE can make plain water taste sweet — a compound in it (cynarin) blocks the sweet receptors, then a sip of water rinses it away and the receptors rebound with a burst of 'sweet.' T3: that's why a glass of water or wine tastes oddly sweet right after eating artichoke. T4: it's also why TOOTHPASTE ruins orange juice — a detergent in toothpaste (SLS) mutes your sweet receptors and strips away a coating that normally tamps down bitterness, so the OJ tastes sourly bitter. T4: all four prove 'sweet' isn't really in the food — it's a receptor signal that molecules can switch on, switch off, or fake.
source: Wikipedia 'Miraculin' (binds hT1R2/hT1R3 sweet receptor, activates only at low pH); Bartoshuk et al., Science 1972 'Sweet Taste of Water Induced by Artichoke (Cynara scolymus)' (cynarin); PMC studies on Gymnema sylvestre gymnemic acids (T1R2/T1R3 sweet-block); 123Dentist / Mental Floss on toothpaste SLS suppressing sweet + disrupting bitter-blocking phospholipids.
framing_note: Wonder voice: lead with the superlative demo ('a berry that turns a raw lemon into candy'). Accuracy rail: all four act on the SWEET receptor (miraculin switches it ON in acid; gymnema, cynarin, and SLS BLOCK it) — the food's actual sugar never changes and every effect is temporary. Dinner-test payoff = the toothpaste-ruins-orange-juice rung (T4), which every kid has already lived.

name: Menthol, the cold that isn't cold
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Why mint feels cold with no ice. T1: mint, peppermint gum, and cooling candies feel COLD in your mouth even though nothing is actually chilled — and a sip of plain water afterward feels icy. T2: menthol (the molecule in mint) tricks TRPM8, the nerve sensor that normally fires when you truly touch something cold — so your brain reports a 'cold' that isn't there. T3: it's the exact MIRROR of chili — capsaicin fakes 'hot' on the heat sensor, menthol fakes 'cold' on the cold sensor — two molecules hijacking your temperature nerves in opposite directions.
source: Bautista et al., Nature 2007 'The menthol receptor TRPM8 is the principal detector of environmental cold' (menthol activates the cold-sensing channel TRPM8); NCBI Bookshelf 'TRPM8: The Cold and Menthol Receptor.'
framing_note: Wonder voice: hook on 'mint makes your mouth feel cold, but a thermometer won't budge.' Accuracy rail: menthol activates the COLD sensor TRPM8 (a temperature nerve), it is NOT a taste; frame it as the clean mirror-image of capsaicin and the heat sensor. Dinner-test payoff = the menthol-is-the-mirror-of-chili rung (T3), which ties this ladder to the capsaicin one.

name: Fat, the sixth basic taste
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Is richness actually a taste? T1: we describe fatty foods as 'creamy' or 'rich,' but scientists now argue FAT has its own basic TASTE, separate from its slippery texture. T1: they even gave it a name — OLEOGUSTUS (Latin oleo, 'oily,' plus gustus, 'taste'). T2: in a careful taste test, people sorted pure fatty-acid samples into their OWN group, apart from sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami — evidence it's a distinct sixth taste. T2: on its own, isolated fat-taste is actually UNPLEASANT (rancid, greasy) — the tongue may be catching spoiled fat, a useful warning. T3: the tongue appears to detect it with a fatty-acid sensor (CD36), the same kind of dedicated-receptor idea behind sweet and umami. T3: so what we LOVE in butter, cream, and marbled steak is mostly the smooth mouthFEEL and aroma — the pure 'taste' of fat is only a faint savory background. T4: a cousin sensation, 'kokumi' ('mouthfulness'), is the round, full, lingering quality certain compounds add to broths and aged cheese — not a taste itself, but a taste-BOOSTER.
source: Running, Craig & Mattes, Chemical Senses 2015 'Oleogustus: The Unique Taste of Fat' (PubMed 26142421; fatty acids sort as a distinct taste; unpleasant in isolation); Purdue University newsroom 2015 release; CD36 as leading candidate fatty-acid taste receptor.
framing_note: Wonder voice: open on 'we call it creamy — but is fat actually a taste?'. Accuracy rail: separate the emerging basic TASTE (oleogustus, via fatty-acid sensors) from the MOUTHFEEL and aroma that make fatty food pleasurable — pure fat-taste is faintly unpleasant, and label oleogustus as a strong recent PROPOSAL, not a fully settled sixth taste. Dinner-test payoff = the 'isolated fat taste is actually gross — a rancid-fat alarm' rung (T2).

name: Temperature and fizz change the taste
strand: The senses & why food tastes that way
scope: Same food, different temperature, different taste. T1: melted ice cream tastes sickly SWEET while frozen ice cream tastes just right — makers OVER-sweeten it on purpose so it isn't bland when eaten cold. T1: warm, flat cola tastes cloying and syrupy, because the chill and the fizz had been hiding how much sugar is really in there. T2: sweetness genuinely gets stronger as food warms — the sweet-signal channel (TRPM5) is heat-sensitive, so a warm bite reads sweeter than an ice-cold one. T3: carbonation isn't only bubbles — an enzyme on your SOUR taste cells turns the drink's CO2 into acid, so 'fizz' is partly a SOUR taste your tongue is reading, not just the pop on your lips.
source: Talavera et al., Nature 2005 'Heat activation of TRPM5 underlies thermal sensitivity of sweet taste' (warming boosts sweet response via TRPM5); Chandrashekar et al., Science 2009 'The Taste of Carbonation' (CO2 sensed as acid via carbonic anhydrase 4 on sour cells).
framing_note: Wonder voice: hook on 'why does melted ice cream taste TOO sweet?'. Accuracy rail: warming really does boost perceived sweetness (heat-sensitive TRPM5), which is why cold desserts and sodas are over-sugared to compensate; carbonation is partly a SOUR taste (CO2 becomes acid on the sour cells), not merely the feel of bubbles. Dinner-test payoff = the melted-ice-cream / deliberately-over-sugared rung (T1).
